secondary_sources: Van Hyning, J.M. (1951). Commercial fish catches of Alaska. USFWS Special Scientific Report No. 68. — The canonical reference for pre-statehood data.

Roppel, P. (1982). Alaska's salmon hatcheries 1891-1959. National Marine Fisheries Service.
Rogers, J.E. (1979). Characteristics of the Alaska salmon purse seine fishery. AFSC Processed Rep.
Cobb, J.N. (1930). Pacific salmon fisheries. USFWS Doc. 1092.

_provenance.notes: The Alaska salmon canning industry began in 1878 with the first cannery at Old Sitka (Southeast AK) and at Klawock. The Karluk River (Kodiak) became the dominant pack site by 1890. At peak, 160+ canneries operated across Alaska. The first salmon hatchery was built at Afognak in 1891 (BCF). All pre-1960 data from Van Hyning (1951) and BCF historical reports.

key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning (1951). Canneries used Chinese immigrant labor. Pack in 48-pound cases.

key_milestones.event: First Nushagak River (Bristol Bay) cannery opens
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning (1951). Start of Bristol Bay commercial fishery.

key_milestones.event: First year Alaska salmon pack exceeds 1 million cases
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning (1951). Explosive growth of cannery industry.

key_milestones.event: First Alaska salmon hatchery opens at Afognak Island
key_milestones.notes: Roppel (1982). BCF-operated. Closed 1936 — deemed unsuccessful by BCF.

key_milestones.event: Alaska Packers Association formed — dominant industry entity
locations: San Francisco HQ, Alaska operations statewide
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning. Controlled ~60% of Alaska pack.

key_milestones.event: Fish traps peak — over 800 fish traps operated in Southeastern Alaska
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning. Fish traps extremely efficient but controversial.

key_milestones.event: Peak of SEAK-dominated era — pack record
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning. SE AK largest producing region at this time.

key_milestones.event: All-Alaska salmon pack record: 6.9 million cases
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning (1951). Pre-regulation peak — unrestricted harvest. Driven by WWI demand.

key_milestones.event: White Act passed — first significant federal salmon conservation law
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning. Restricted traps, established escapement requirements. Inadequately enforced.

key_milestones.event: Salmon pack near 7 million cases — near all-time record
WWII canning demand surges — military rations
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning. Military demand replaces export market.

key_milestones.event: Salmon pack at historic low — stocks severely depleted
key_milestones.notes: Van Hyning. 30+ years of unrestricted overfishing has crashed Alaska salmon.

key_milestones.event: Alaska statehood — fish traps immediately banned
key_milestones.notes: ADF&G. First act of new Alaska legislature bans all fish traps — ending 80 years of trap fishing. Major power shift from outside cannery interests to local fishermen.
ADF&G. Restricted access begins. Commercial fishing rights become property.

key_milestones.event: Magnuson-Stevens FCMA — 200-mile EEZ eliminates foreign fleets
key_milestones.notes: NOAA. Japanese and Soviet fleets operating inside 200 miles excluded. US domestic fleet expansion begins.

key_milestones.event: Global salmon price crash — farmed Atlantic salmon floods market
key_milestones.notes: ADF&G/ASMI. Sockeye ex-vessel price falls below $0.25/lb. Many fishermen lose money. Some canneries close.

key_milestones.event: BB drift gillnet permits worth $42,000 — lowest ever
key_milestones.notes: CFEC. Industry crisis. Congressional fisheries disaster declared.

key_milestones.event: Bristol Bay 62.3M sockeye — shatters all records
key_milestones.notes: ADF&G. Industry fully recovered from 1999 crash. Strong market, strong prices, record volume.

key_milestones.event: Bristol Bay 79.8M sockeye — all-time world record wild sockeye
key_milestones.notes: ADF&G. $326M ex-vessel value for BB alone — more valuable than all of Alaska salmon in 2001.

cannery_counts_by_era.notes: Van Hyning. Decline due to overfishing.
ADF&G. Modern consolidated processing sector. Many are floating processors.
